summary:
This A/B evaluation covered two chat-based diagnostic evals ("bedrock-agent-empty-response" and "agentcore-runtime-cannot-invoke"), each run 3 times per variant, with no failed runs.

Trigger firing: In both evals, the behavior under test fired 100% of the time (3/3), so the eval scenarios were reliably exercised for both variants.

Expected output: Neither variant met the defined "expected output" criterion in either eval (0/3 for with_skill and without_skill in both cases). This measurement has high confidence, so it's a consistent finding rather than a noisy one — both variants are missing the same target output bar, not just one of them.

Per-assertion detail (this is where most of the signal is):
- In "bedrock-agent-empty-response" (18 assertions each): both variants pass the same three assertions 100% of the time (alias resolution, guardrail-routing, concrete ordered checks) and both always fail two assertions (findings lacking severity/evidence support; missing AGT/AC catalog check-id) — these two always-fail assertions suggest the tested behavior or the assertion itself needs work, independent of variant. One assertion (no raw 12-digit account ID exposed) was flaky for both, passing 0/3 for with_skill and 1/3 for without_skill. Overall assertion pass rate was close: with_skill 50% (9/18) vs without_skill 56% (10/18).
- In "agentcore-runtime-cannot-invoke" (21 assertions each): one assertion (SCP deny consideration) passes 100% for both variants, and one (AGT/AC catalog check-id) always fails for both — again pointing to a gap independent of variant. Several assertions are flaky and show a consistent direction favoring with_skill: simulating/inspecting runtime role permissions (1/3 vs 0/3), checking VPC endpoints (2/3 vs 1/3), and disclosing AgentCore read-permission gaps (2/3 vs 0/3) all passed more often for with_skill. One flaky assertion (masking account IDs in ARNs, medium confidence) also favored with_skill (2/3 vs 1/3), while the simpler regex check for raw account-ID exposure favored without_skill (3/3 vs 2/3). Overall assertion pass rate here was wider: with_skill 57% (12/21) vs without_skill 38% (8/21).

Quality comparison: No head-to-head quality pairs were evaluated for either eval (all 3 pairs skipped in each), so there is no quality-comparison data to weigh alongside the assertion results.

Runtime and cost: without_skill was consistently faster and cheaper than with_skill in both evals — roughly 8s/$0.07 vs 23s/$0.20 in the empty-response eval, and 15s/$0.13 vs 22s/$0.19 in the cannot-invoke eval. Context window utilization was similar and low for both (under 6%), with no compaction events.

Output consistency: In the empty-response eval, with_skill's outputs were rated fully "consistent" (score 3.0) across runs, while without_skill was "mostly_consistent" (score 2.33). In the cannot-invoke eval, both were "mostly_consistent" with similar scores (with_skill 2.67, without_skill 2.33). Confidence in these consistency judgments was high in both evals.

Overall, the picture is mixed rather than one-sided: trigger firing and the (failing) expected-output measure are identical across variants and both evals show assertions that pass or fail identically for both variants, indicating some underlying behaviors/assertions apply regardless of variant. Where differences do appear, with_skill tends to show somewhat higher assertion pass rates (notably in the cannot-invoke eval) and slightly more run-to-run consistency, while without_skill is notably faster and lower-cost in both evals. With no quality-pair data available, these runtime/cost savings versus assertion-pass differences represent a tradeoff rather than a clear overall difference.

bedrock-agent-empty-response.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task (3 repeated runs) about diagnosing why a Bedrock agent produces empty output. The trigger behavior under test fired reliably in all 3 runs (100%), so the scenario was properly exercised.

Expected-output match: both with_skill and without_skill failed to meet the defined expected output in all 3 runs (0/3 each), and this was measured with high confidence, so it's a clear, reliable finding that neither variant currently satisfies the full expected-output bar — this is a shared gap, not a difference between the two.

Assertion-level detail (18 assertion checks total per variant, from 6 distinct assertions x 3 runs) shows a mixed picture rather than a uniform gap:
- Three assertions passed 3/3 for both variants (alias resolution before assuming production state, checking guardrail attachment while deferring policy-content questions, and naming concrete ordered checks rather than generic advice). These are not differentiating — both variants handle them equally well.
- One assertion ("each finding carries a severity and concrete observed signal") failed for both variants in all runs — this looks like a shared weakness in both outputs (or a hard-to-satisfy assertion) rather than something separating the two.
- One assertion ("at least one finding carries an AGT/AC catalog check-id") also failed for both variants in all runs — another shared gap.
- One assertion ("no raw 12-digit account ID is exposed") was flaky: with_skill failed all 3 runs (0/3) while without_skill passed 1 of 3 runs (33%). This is the only assertion where the two variants diverged, and even there without_skill's pass rate was low and inconsistent rather than solid.

Overall assertion pass rates were close: with_skill passed 9/18 (50%) vs without_skill 10/18 (56%), a small difference driven mainly by the one flaky account-ID assertion.

Quality comparison: no head-to-head quality pairs could actually be scored (0 evaluated, all 3 skipped), so there is no quality-based signal to weigh here — this dimension is simply absent data.

Runtime and cost: with_skill averaged ~23s and ~$0.20 per run, while without_skill averaged ~8s and ~$0.07 per run — without_skill was notably faster and cheaper in this test, with similar (low) context-window utilization for both (~4-5%, no compaction for either).

Output consistency across repeated runs: with_skill was rated fully "consistent" across all 3 scored dimensions (score 3.0, high confidence). without_skill was rated "mostly_consistent" overall (score 2.33, high confidence), with 1 of 3 dimensions fully consistent and 2 only mostly consistent — suggesting without_skill's outputs varied a bit more run-to-run than with_skill's.

In sum: both variants fail the expected-output bar and share the same two failing assertions and the same three passing assertions, so most of the assertion evidence does not differentiate them. The one place they diverge (account-ID exposure) favors without_skill but only marginally and inconsistently. Variant_b ran faster and cheaper, while with_skill showed slightly steadier output consistency across runs. No quality-comparison data was available. These are tradeoffs across speed/cost versus run-to-run consistency, set against a shared underlying expected-output gap, rather than a clear overall difference between the two variants.

agentcore-runtime-cannot-invoke.summary:
This eval tested a single chat task across 3 runs each. The trigger behavior under test fired reliably (3/3), confirming the test scenario itself worked as intended.

Expected output: Both without_skill and with_skill failed to meet the expected output in all 3 runs (0/3 for each), and this judgment was made with high confidence (not a low-confidence artifact). So on the primary pass/fail criterion, both variants performed equally poorly — this is a case where neither variant succeeded, pointing to a shared weakness (or a very demanding expected-output bar) rather than a difference between the two.

Assertion-level detail (21 individual assertion checks per variant) tells a more nuanced story, since partial credit differs even though full expected-output success was 0 for both:
- Overall pass rate: with_skill passed 12/21 (57%), without_skill passed 8/21 (38%) — with_skill passed more assertions in aggregate.
- One assertion ("explicit SCP deny considered as a cause...") passed 3/3 for both variants — this check doesn't differentiate them.
- One assertion ("finding carries an AGT or AC catalog check-id") failed 0/3 for both variants — this is a shared gap, suggesting either the behavior or the assertion itself needs attention, not a difference between variants.
- Several assertions showed with_skill outperforming without_skill: inspecting runtime execution role permissions (1/3 vs 0/3), checking VPC endpoints (2/3 vs 1/3), disclosing AgentCore read denials under default policy (2/3 vs 0/3), and masking account segments in ARNs (2/3 vs 1/3, medium confidence).
- One assertion reversed: "No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed" (regex-based) passed 3/3 for without_skill but only 2/3 for with_skill — a case where without_skill did better.
Most of these differentiating assertions are marked "flaky" (inconsistent pass/fail across the 3 runs for at least one variant), so the per-assertion differences should be read with some caution regarding run-to-run stability.

Quality comparison: No side-by-side quality pairs could be evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 3 skipped), so there is no data on relative output quality between the variants for this eval.

Runtime/cost: without_skill ran faster (~15s vs ~22s) and cheaper (~$0.13 vs ~$0.19) than with_skill. Context window utilization was similar and low for both (~5%), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency: Both variants were rated "mostly_consistent" overall, with high confidence. with_skill scored slightly higher (2.67, with 2 of 3 dimensions fully consistent) versus without_skill (2.33, with 1 of 3 dimensions fully consistent) — a modest difference in run-to-run stability favoring with_skill.

Overall, this is a mixed and fairly low-certainty picture: both variants failed the full expected-output bar entirely, several assertions are shared failures or flaky, and no quality-pair comparison exists. Where differences appear, with_skill passed more individual assertions and was marginally more consistent, while without_skill was faster, cheaper, and won on one specific regex-based account-masking assertion. These appear as tradeoffs rather than a clear overall difference.
